summary: For ages 7–8: solve multiplication/division problems involving SCALING ('n times as big/many', a multiplicative enlargement distinct from additive 'n more') and CORRESPONDENCE (n objects each paired with m objects, e.g. 3 tops × 4 bottoms = 12 outfits, or 4 shirts × 3 trousers = 12), plus the inverse missing-number/division versions. Learners manipulate bars to see scaling as multiplying not adding, build organised pairings or arrays for correspondence, and work backward from a scaled quantity to the original.
misconceptions: Treating scaling additively: reading '3 times as tall' as '3 cm/units taller' rather than ×3.
Undercounting correspondence combinations by not being systematic (missing pairings).
Not recognising a correspondence problem as multiplication at all.
Confusing which quantity is scaled and by how much in comparison problems.
Ignoring the inverse: unable to work backward from the scaled quantity to the original (the division version).

activities.title: Stretch the bar: 'times as tall' versus 'taller'
steps: Draw or stretch a bar to make it a chosen number of times as long as an 8 cm original bar (e.g. ×3).
Alongside, place a second 'additive' comparison bar that is only 3 units longer than the original, and compare the two end points.
State and solve: 'A blue ribbon is 3 times as long as a red ribbon that is 8 cm — how long is the blue one?' (answer 24 cm).
Then reverse it: given a bar that is 3 times as long and measures 18 cm, find the original length (18 ÷ 3 = 6 cm).
Say aloud why '3 times as long' means three copies, not 'longer by 3'.
activities.insight: 'n times as big' is multiplicative — it makes that many copies of the quantity — so for this original of 8 cm the ×3 bar (24 cm) ends up well beyond the +3 bar (11 cm); the size of that gap depends on the original (it is not universally true that 'times' exceeds 'plus' for every original and factor), and the inverse of scaling is division.

activities.title: Every outfit: building correspondence as an array
steps: Solve: 'You have 4 shirts and 3 pairs of trousers — how many different outfits can you make?'
Make an organised list or draw lines pairing each shirt with each of the 3 pairs of trousers, so no pairing is missed.
Arrange the completed pairings into a 4×3 (or 3×4) array and count the cells to confirm 12 outfits.
Change one quantity (e.g. 5 pairs of trousers, giving 4 × 5 = 20) and rebuild to see how the total changes.
Explain why the answer is 4 × 3, not 4 + 3.
activities.insight: Correspondence (each of n paired with each of m) is the same multiplication structure as an array; working systematically finds all combinations and prevents undercounting.

activities.title: Fill the box: missing factors and the inverse
steps: Solve the missing-number problem 6 × □ = 42 by asking 'six times WHAT is 42?' and using a known fact or 42 ÷ 6.
Check the answer (□ = 7) by multiplying back: 6 × 7 = 42.
Create and solve a missing-number scaling problem, e.g. 'The tower is 3 times as tall and 18 cm — how tall is the original?' (6 cm).
Explain how multiplication and division undo each other here.
activities.insight: A missing factor is found with a known fact or by division, not by adding or subtracting; multiplication and division are inverses.

activities.title: Sort and match: which structure is this?
steps: For each word problem, decide whether it is scaling or correspondence, whether the unknown is the result or a missing number (such as the original length or a missing factor), and which operation it needs.
Match a correspondence problem to the array that represents it.
Spot and correct a tempting wrong answer, e.g. choosing '11 cm' for '3 times as long as 8 cm' or '7 outfits' for 4 shirts and 3 trousers.
activities.insight: Recognising the multiplicative structure across its varied forms (scaling, correspondence, missing factor, the last solved by division) is an important part of the objective, alongside building representations and solving the problems.

checkQuestion: Give the child these to solve while you watch the set-up: (scaling) 'A blue ribbon is 3 times as long as a red ribbon that is 8 cm — how long is the blue one?'; (correspondence) 'You have 4 shirts and 3 pairs of trousers. How many different outfits can you make?'; (missing number) 'Fill in the box: 6 × □ = 42.' Watch which operation they choose for each.
checkAnswer: 24 cm (3 × 8, scaling); 12 outfits (4 × 3, correspondence); □ = 7 (missing factor, via 42 ÷ 6 or knowing 6×7). The teacher watches for multiplication on the scaling and correspondence problems and use of a known fact / inverse for the missing number.
